Builds on [post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) and on [post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd)'s pitch ruler. Deep dives hold the equations and derivations. About 20 minutes. Written in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.
:::

[]{#orchestra}Struck or plucked and left to ring, most instruments sound at the frequencies of their own eigenvalues: a little sharp of the whole-number lines on a piano, far off them on a kalimba, between them on a drum. Bowed, blown or, like the theremin, kept going by a circuit, they sound exactly on the lines. Below, one instrument from each of the five [Hornbostel–Sachs](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hornbostel-sachs) classes, sorted by what makes the sound,[^hs] plays Grieg,[^grieg] every voice built from the spectra on this page.

```{=html}
Simplified: no breath, bow or stick noise; the glockenspiel's overtone fading times are illustrative; a real theremin is not a pure sine.</p>
<p><b>The cards, as text.</b> <i>Where the stems come from.</i> Musicologists sort instruments into five classes by what makes the sound (Hornbostel and Sachs, 1914; electrophones added later). One recipe turns each into its stems. (1) For small motions, Newton's law on a small piece of the instrument takes the form u<sub>tt</sub> = −Au: u is the instrument's shape, and the operator A turns a shape into minus the acceleration it causes. (2) A shape that the operator only stretches, AX = λX, swings at one frequency, f = √λ / 2π. (3) Left to ring, every motion is a sum of such shapes (for a bounded object without friction; post 2 proves it for the string, and the fold under “The same recipe” gives the theorem for the others), so the list of the λ's, the spectrum of the operator, decides where the stems stand.</p>
<p><i>Electrophone, sine theremin.</i> Kirchhoff's law on a coil and a capacitor; operator A = 1/LC, a single number, like a mass on a spring; spectrum f = 1/(2π√(LC)). One stem: a pure tone. A real theremin runs two such circuits at radio frequencies, the hand changing C of one, and you hear the difference of their frequencies, with overtones.</p>
<p><i>Chordophone, piano.</i> Newton's law on a short piece of stiff steel wire; operator A = −c² d²/dx² + κ² d⁴/dx⁴, ends pinned; spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = n f<sub>0</sub> √(1 + Bn²). Just above the lines, more so as n grows: a note, slightly stretched.</p>
<p><i>Aerophone, clarinet.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of the air in the tube; operator A = −c² d²/dx² on pressure, closed at the reed and open at the far end; the tube's spectrum f<sub>n</sub> = (2n − 1) c / 4L. Blown, the air repeats one cycle, so the partials sit exactly on the lines; the tube's odd modes make the odd ones strong and the even ones weak: a hollow note.</p>
<p><i>Idiophone, glockenspiel.</i> Newton's law on a thin slice of a steel bar; operator A = κ² d⁴/dx⁴, both ends free; spectrum from cos βL cosh βL = 1, ratios 1 : 2.76 : 5.40. Off the lines, but the overtones die fast: a bright, clean note.</p>
<p><i>Membranophones, bass drum and timpani.</i> Newton's law on a small patch of the drumhead; operator A = −c²Δ, rim held still; spectrum from J<sub>m</sub>(ka) = 0, ratios 1 : 1.59 : 2.14 : 2.30 …; the timpani's spectrum is measured, not derived. Bass drum: struck off centre, mostly round modes, off the lines and fading fast: a boom with no clear pitch. Timpani: the same skin; the air it drags along pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the stroke favours them and the round modes fade fast: a note.</p>
<p><i>Every sound in this video was built from pure tones at these spectra. No recordings, no samples.</i> Made in collaboration with Claude, Anthropic's AI model.</p>
<p><b>About the player.</b> It plays a sine theremin (electrophone), a piano (chordophone), a clarinet (aerophone), a glockenspiel (idiophone), and two membranophones, a bass drum and a kettledrum (timpani). The struck notes fade, at frequencies computed from each instrument's operator (the bass drum's from the ideal drumhead of the <a href="#drums">drums entry</a>), except the kettledrum's, which are measured, because the <a href="drum.html">drum page</a>'s toy model gets only halfway to them; the fading times are illustrative. The clarinet holds a steady tone with the tube's odd multiples strong and the even ones faint, and the theremin a single steady pure tone. Each lane shows its current note's frequencies on the pitch ruler of post 1, whose gray lines are whole-number multiples of one frequency. The arrangement is ours, after the transcription at <a href="https://flutetunes.com/tunes.php?id=91">flutetunes.com</a>. On a small screen, use Full screen with the phone turned sideways.</p>
</details></div>
```

The reason, in one sentence: **a ringing instrument moves as a sum of its own modes, as the string does, so you hear its spectrum; a bowed or blown one is pushed into one repeating cycle, and a repeating cycle has only whole-number partials.**

## The same recipe {#recipe}

Every instrument below is a problem of the same shape as the string's: an equation, how the object is held, and how it starts or is driven. For the ones left to ring, the string's argument carries over to every bounded object here: each has its own shapes, the [eigenfunctions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#eigenfunction) of its operator, and every motion is a sum of them, each swinging at $f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi$, apart from the glockenspiel's two drifts, its slide and tilt, which move as $a + bt$. The exception is the kettledrum: its sound radiates into the unbounded air around it, which takes it outside this argument (see the fold), so its ratios here are measured.[^benade]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The theorem, and its three names <span class="needs">uses Hilbert spaces</span></summary>

What carries over from the string: on a bounded object with a reasonable edge, each of these operators is [self-adjoint](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-adjoint) and $\geq 0$ and has a [compact resolvent](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#compact-resolvent), so it has an [orthonormal basis](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#orthonormal) of eigenfunctions, and drifts split off. The three routes are Sturm–Liouville theory for strings and tubes, a compact [Green's operator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#green) for bars, and Rellich's theorem for drums (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, [*Methods of Mathematical Physics*, vol. 1](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/naturwissenschaften/methods-of-mathematical-physics-978-3-527-41447-5), Interscience, 1953, chapters III (symmetric kernels), V and VI; L. C. Evans, [*Partial Differential Equations*](https://bookstore.ams.org/GSM/19.R), 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, sections 5.7 and 6.5.1). The kettledrum's radiation, sound carried away into the unbounded air, makes its problem non-self-adjoint, and its full air loading is beyond this page; the air's added mass alone would keep it inside the theorem, as the drum page's toy model of the air does.

A *Sturm–Liouville problem* is $-(p\,X')' + q\,X = \lambda\,w\,X$ on a bounded interval, with $p, w > 0$ and one condition at each end of the form $\alpha X + \beta X' = 0$; the string ($p = c^2$, $q = 0$, $w = 1$) and the tubes, open or closed at each end, are of this form, and its eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis (R. Courant and D. Hilbert, [*Methods of Mathematical Physics*, vol. 1](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/naturwissenschaften/methods-of-mathematical-physics-978-3-527-41447-5), Interscience, 1953, chapters V and VI). For a bar, $(A + 1)^{-1}$ is an integral operator with a kernel continuous on $[0, L]^2$, the Green's operator, which is compact and self-adjoint, so the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators applies to it, and its eigenfunctions are $A$'s. For a drumhead, Rellich's theorem says that on a bounded region, every sequence of shapes that vanish on the rim and have $\iint u^2$ and $\iint |\nabla u|^2$ bounded has a subsequence converging in mean square; this makes $(A + 1)^{-1}$ compact (L. C. Evans, [*Partial Differential Equations*](https://bookstore.ams.org/GSM/19.R), 2nd ed., American Mathematical Society, 2010, section 5.7). A drift occurs only when $A$ has the eigenvalue 0: on this page, for the glockenspiel bar.

</details>
:::

## Two kinds of entry {#two-kinds}

A *ringing* entry is struck or plucked, then left alone: its partials sit wherever its spectrum falls, each fading at its own rate.

A *self-sustained* entry is kept going by the player, with a bow, an air jet, a reed or an amplifier, whose push depends on the motion itself, not in proportion to it.[^drive] Its motion settles into one repeating cycle, a [self-sustained oscillation](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#self-sustained), so its partials are exact whole-number multiples ([post 1](../what-you-hear/index.qmd#why-whole-numbers-repeat)), whatever the spectrum of the driven part, the [resonator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#resonator); the drive and the resonator decide only which partials are strong.

In every demo the stems are the sound's partials on the pitch ruler, taller when stronger, and the picture is slowed down and enlarged.

## A piano {#piano}

A piano note is clear, but its upper partials run slightly sharp of the whole-number lines, more so the higher they are, because the steel wire resists bending as well as being pulled straight.[^fr12] So an exact 2 : 1 octave [beats](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beats), and tuners widen octaves, most at the keyboard's ends.[^railsback]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="piano">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A piano wire between two pins, swinging in its first twelve modes"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The piano note's partials, each a little sharp of its whole-number line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">Middle C, struck an eighth of the way along (books commonly give 1/7 to 1/9, though on modern pianos many notes are struck nearer the end: <a href="https://www.speech.kth.se/music/5_lectures/conklin/whereshould.html">Conklin</a>), where the 8th mode stands still, so in the model its stem is zero. Computed: the stem positions, with B = 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, a rough value for a middle C wire. Modelled: each mode starts in proportion to its height under the hammer, with a roll-off for the felt. Illustrative: the fading times.</p>
</div></div>
```

The spectrum is $f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}$, where $B$ measures the wire's stiffness, about $4.4\times10^{-4}$ for a middle C wire. The player controls the hammer's speed (harder is louder and brighter),[^russell] the dampers and the pedals; none of them moves a frequency ([A Piano](../a-piano/index.qmd)).

**[Deep dive: the piano →](piano.qmd)**

## A kalimba {#kalimba}

A kalimba tine gives a click, then a clean note: its first overtone, far off the lines and strong at the attack, dies within a fraction of a second.[^chapman] The thumb bends the tine into a smooth curve and lets go.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="kalimba">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A kalimba tine clamped on the left, released from a bent shape and swinging"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The tine's partials at 1, 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest frequency, off the whole-number lines"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A tine at A4, 440 Hz, pushed at its tip and let go. Computed: the stem positions and each stem's starting height, the push on the bridge (the shear force at the clamp) from the smooth bent start (a cubic, derived on the kalimba page). Illustrative: the fading times, chosen to match <a href="https://acoustics.org/pressroom/httpdocs/155th/chapman.htm">Chapman</a>'s observation that the overtones die within a fraction of a second; the stems shrink as each partial fades. The tine is drawn as it moves; in displacement its first overtone is only 2.5% of the fundamental, so the picture shows mostly the first mode, while in the push on the bridge it starts at 55%.</p>
</div></div>
```

The spectrum is in the ratios $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, and $f_1 \propto 1/L^2$: half the length sounds two octaves up.[^fr2] The player sets the loudness by how far the tip is pushed and can stop a tine with a finger; makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge.[^kmagic]

**[Deep dive: the kalimba →](kalimba.qmd)**

## A glockenspiel {#glockenspiel}

A glockenspiel gives a bright, clear note although its overtones sit off the lines: they are high and die quickly, leaving the fundamental.[^scavone] Its bar is the same kind of steel bar as the kalimba's tine, with both ends [free](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#free-end); it rests on soft supports and is struck with a mallet.
$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -\kappa^2u_{xxxx} \quad (0 < x < L), \\
u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 \ \text{ at } x = 0 \text{ and } x = L, \\
u(x, 0) = 0, \qquad u_t(x, 0) = v_0(x).
\end{gathered}
$$
Here $\kappa^2$ is the bar's stiffness over its mass, and $v_0$ the mallet's blow (fold).

The spectrum is in the ratios $1 : 2.756 : 5.404$, off the lines, from $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$.[^fr19a] It also has two eigenvalues 0, the bar sliding or tilting without bending: *drifts*, which move as $a + bt$ instead of swinging and make no sound.

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="glockenspiel">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A glockenspiel bar on two supports, swinging in its first three modes"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bar's partials at 1, 2.76 and 5.40 times its lowest frequency, off the whole-number lines"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A bar tuned to C6, 1047 Hz, struck a little off its middle. Computed: the stem positions. Illustrative: the starting strengths and the fading times. The bar is drawn on its two supports, at its fundamental's still points.</p>
</div></div>
```

The supports, at the fundamental's still points $0.224L$ from each end, barely damp it.[^ubc1] Xylophone and marimba bars, unlike glockenspiel bars, are thinned underneath to put the first overtone on a line, 3× and 4×.[^fr19b] The player sets the loudness by the blow, the brightness by the mallet, metal brighter and rubber warmer,[^mallet] and stops a note with a hand; some glockenspiels on a stand have a damper pedal.[^vsl]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Here $\kappa^2 = EI/\rho S$: $E$ is steel's [Young's modulus](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#youngs-modulus), $I$ the [second moment of area](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#second-moment) of the cross-section, $\rho$ the density and $S$ the cross-section's area; $v_0$ is the mallet's blow, concentrated where it lands. The equation is the kalimba tine's [beam](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beam) equation, from the same slice of bar (derived on the [kalimba page](kalimba.qmd#newton)). Only the ends differ: on soft supports both ends are free, so at each end no bending moment and no shear force act, $u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0$. The supports are taken as not holding the bar at all; resting at the fundamental's still points, they are where that mode does not move.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The spectrum, step by step <span class="needs">uses a 2×2 determinant</span></summary>

With $\lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4$, $X = b_1\cos\beta x + b_2\sin\beta x + b_3\cosh\beta x + b_4\sinh\beta x$. The free left end, $X''(0) = X'''(0) = 0$, gives $b_3 = b_1$ and $b_4 = b_2$. With $c_1 = \cos\beta L$, $s_1 = \sin\beta L$, $c_2 = \cosh\beta L$ and $s_2 = \sinh\beta L$ ([hyperbolic functions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hyperbolic)), the free right end gives $(c_2 - c_1)b_1 + (s_2 - s_1)b_2 = 0$ and $(s_2 + s_1)b_1 + (c_2 - c_1)b_2 = 0$, whose determinant is $(c_2 - c_1)^2 - (s_2^2 - s_1^2) = 2 - 2c_1c_2$. So $\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = 1$, with roots $\beta L = 4.7300, 7.8532, 10.9956, \dots$ For $\lambda = 0$, $X'''' = 0$ with free ends leaves exactly $X = a + bx$: two eigenfunctions with eigenvalue 0, whose coordinates move as $q = a + bt$. The fundamental's still points, where $X_1 = 0$, are at $0.224L$ and $0.776L$ (computed).

</details>
:::

## Drums {#drums}

A bass drum booms with no clear pitch; a kettledrum, one of the timpani, plays a note. Both heads are a stretched skin whose ideal frequencies fall between the lines;[^fr3] on the kettledrum the air pulls the spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base, and the round modes radiate away within a fraction of a second.[^hpt1] Step through it:

```{=html}
  </div>

    <div class="hd">Bass drum <span class="v" id="tdVb"></span><button type="button" id="tdPb">▶ Play</button><button type="button" id="tdMuf" aria-pressed="false" title="Muffle the head with a leg or a towel: every mode fades fast, for a short note">Muffle</button></div>
    <canvas class="head" id="tdHb" role="img" aria-label="The bass drum's head seen from above, with the point where it is struck."></canvas>
    <canvas class="sp" id="tdSb" role="img" aria-label="The bass drum's spectrum diagram."></canvas>
  </div>
  <div class="drum">
    <div class="hd">Timpani <span class="v" id="tdVt"></span><button type="button" id="tdPt">▶ Play</button><button type="button" id="tdM" aria-pressed="false" title="Play the spoke modes at the measured pattern 2, 3, 4, 5 times the base instead of this toy model's values">Measured ratios</button></div>
    <canvas class="head" id="tdHt" role="img" aria-label="The timpani's head seen from above, with the point where it is struck."></canvas>
    <canvas class="sp" id="tdSt" role="img" aria-label="The timpani's spectrum diagram."></canvas>
  </div>
  <details class="more">
    <summary>Try other values</summary>
    <div class="slider"><label for="tdR">Timpani strike point, fraction of the radius</label><input type="range" id="tdR" min="0" max="0.95" step="0.01" value="0.62"><output id="tdRo"></output></div>
    <div class="slider"><label for="tdMu">Air's added mass, 2ρa/σ</label><input type="range" id="tdMu" min="0" max="8" step="0.05" value="3.03"><output id="tdMuo"></output></div>
    <div class="slider"><label for="tdK">Kettle stiffness (raises the lowest round mode's λ by this fraction)</label><input type="range" id="tdK" min="0" max="2" step="0.05" value="1"><output id="tdKo"></output></div>
  </details>
  <p class="cap">Each stem is one mode: its position is its frequency as a multiple of a base an octave below the (1,1) mode, so the (1,1) sits at 2×, and its height is how strongly the strike starts it; dashed stems are modes that have faded. Stems on the dashed whole-number lines make a note. Each drum plays at its own size: the bass drum's lowest mode near 50 Hz, the timpani's (1,1) at 131 Hz (C3). Measured ratios puts the kettledrum's spoke modes on 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 times the base, the pattern a kettledrum measured by Benade sits close to (about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times its lowest mode, as tabulated by <a href="https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Music/timpani.html">HyperPhysics</a>), which this toy model gets only halfway to. Computed: the ideal head's frequencies and the strike weights. Modelled: the air's mass and the kettle, in the simple forms given on the <a href="drum.html">drum page</a>. Illustrative: the fading times.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

The ideal head's spectrum is in the ratios $1 : 1.593 : 2.136 : 2.295 : \cdots$, from the zeros of [Bessel functions](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#bessel). The bass drummer strikes slightly off center and shortens the note by muffling the head with a leg or a towel;[^aleo] the timpanist strikes between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, and retunes by changing the head's tension, usually with a pedal.[^hpt3]

**[Deep dive: the drum →](drum.qmd)**

## A violin, bowed {#violin}

A bowed string holds a steady note with its partials exactly on the lines: the bow's friction grabs the string and lets it slip once per period, so the string repeats one cycle, which Helmholtz watched through a vibration microscope by 1860.[^helm]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="violin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A bowed string: two straight pieces joined by a corner that races between the nut and the bridge"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The bowed sound's partials on every whole-number line, with the string's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">Helmholtz motion of an open G string, 196 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, computed for the ideal string, with strength 1/n, without the wooden body. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the string's modes, on every line too. The picture is the sum of the first 40 modes; dashed, the corner's path, two arcs of a parabola.</p>
</div></div>
```

The string's own spectrum is post 2's, $f_n = nf_1$; the bowed sound's partials sit on the same lines, partial $n$ pushing the bridge in proportion to $1/n$ (derived on the violin page). The left hand chooses the length and adds vibrato; the bow's speed, force and distance from the bridge set the loudness and brightness.[^wolfebow2]

**[Deep dive: the violin →](violin.qmd)**

## A flute {#flute}

A flute plays a steady note on the lines; with every hole closed and an ever faster airstream, it climbs the harmonic series, 1, 2, 3, 4, … times the lowest.[^wolfefl1] It is a tube of air open at both ends, kept going by a jet blown across the embouchure hole.[^fr16] An open end holds room pressure, so the tube's spectrum has the string's numbers, $f_n = nc/2L$, on every line.[^pipes1]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="flute">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube open at both ends, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The flute's partials on every whole-number line, with the open tube's own frequencies marked under the axis, also on every line"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D4, 294 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, all on the lines; their strengths, 1/n², are an illustrative choice. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the open tube's modes, on every line too. Picture: the air in the tube, darker where the pressure is higher, with thin slabs of air that bunch where it is squeezed.</p>
</div></div>
```

The player chooses the length with the keys, the loudness with the breath, and the register with that faster, narrower airstream.[^wolfefl2]

**[Deep dive: the flute, on the clarinet page →](clarinet.qmd)**

## A clarinet {#clarinet}

A clarinet sounds a hollow note nearly an octave below a flute of the same length. Its tube is closed at the reed, which halves the lowest frequency and leaves only odd multiples of it, so in the low register the odd partials are strong and the even ones weak.[^ovc1]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="clarinet">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="The air in a tube closed at the reed on the left and open at the bell, shaded by pressure, with thin slabs of air moving back and forth"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The clarinet's partials on every whole-number line, strong odd ones and faint even ones, with the tube's own frequencies marked under the axis on the odd lines only"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A steady D3, 147 Hz. Stems: the sound's partials, on every line, strong odd and faint even ones; the exact strengths are an illustrative choice after Wolfe's description. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the tube's modes, on the odd lines only. Picture: the air column, closed at the reed on the left, drawn with the odd partials only; the faint even ones are left out of the picture.</p>
</div></div>
```

The tube's spectrum is $f_n = (2n - 1)c/4L$, the odd multiples of $c/4L$.[^pipes2] The fingers choose the length, the breath the loudness and brightness, and the register key jumps the tube to its next mode, 3 times the lowest: a twelfth up, where a flute overblows an octave.[^wolfecl3]

**[Deep dive: the clarinet →](clarinet.qmd)**

## A harmonica {#harmonica}

A harmonica reed's own overtones sit far off the lines, yet its note has partials only on the lines, odd and even both strong. You hear the air, not the reed: the reed lets one identical puff through its slot per cycle, and repeating puffs have only whole-number partials.[^pykett1]

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="harmonica">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A reed riveted over its slot, swinging through it and letting out one puff of air per cycle, with a trace of the airflow"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="The blown reed's partials on every whole-number line, with the reed's own frequencies marked under the axis at 1 and 6.27 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">A C5 reed, 523 Hz, blown. Stems: the sound's partials, at whole-number multiples of the playing frequency, computed from the puff drawn on the right: one puff per cycle, open for about 30% of it, a shape chosen for illustration. Ticks under the axis: the resonator's own frequencies, the reed's modes, at 1 and 6.27 times its lowest; the playing frequency sits somewhat below the lowest, drawn here at 1. The reed is drawn in its first mode, and the slot is drawn open only while the tip is above the plate.</p>
</div></div>
```

The reed's spectrum is the kalimba tine's, $1 : 6.27 : 17.55$, and it plays somewhat below its lowest mode.[^cott] The breath sets the loudness and the tone while the pitch hardly moves;[^pykett3] on a diatonic harmonica, reshaping mouth and throat bends a note down between the hole's two notes, because the hole's blow and draw reeds both take part.[^bahnson]

**[Deep dive: the harmonica →](harmonica.qmd)**

## A theremin {#theremin}

A theremin is played without being touched, and its tone glides as the hand moves.[^thm1] It makes the tone with electric circuits, each a coil and a capacitor, an [LC circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LC_circuit), whose charge swings like a mass on a spring:
$$
\ddot q = -\frac{1}{LC}\,q .
$$
Here $q$ is the charge, $L$ the coil's [inductance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#inductance) and $C$ the [capacitance](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#capacitance) (fold). An amplifier keeps the circuit swinging at a steady size.[^osc]

The spectrum is one frequency, $f = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$, a radio frequency below 500 kHz.[^thm2] The instrument runs two such circuits, one changed by the player's hand, and outputs the difference of their frequencies, which is audible ([heterodyning](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#heterodyning)).

```{=html}
<div class="ins"><div class="panel gdemo" data-g="theremin">
  <canvas class="gsk" role="img" aria-label="A coil and a capacitor, with the charge sloshing between the capacitor's plates"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" role="img" aria-label="One partial, at 1 times"></svg>
  <div class="controls"><button type="button" class="primary" data-gplay>▶ Play</button><span class="cap">motion slowed and enlarged</span></div>
  <p class="cap">An idealized sine theremin at A4, 440 Hz: one stem. A real theremin's tone is not a pure sine: it has overtones. No resonator ticks: the circuits' own frequencies are radio frequencies, far beyond this ruler, and the tone you hear is the difference of two of them. Picture: one coil-and-capacitor circuit, its charge sloshing between the plates, slowed to about one swing a second.</p>
</div></div>
```

Most players set the pitch with the right hand's distance from one antenna and the loudness with the left hand's from the other. Leon Theremin invented it in 1920 and patented it in 1928.[^thm3]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Where the equation comes from</summary>

Here $q$ is the charge on the capacitor, $L$ the coil's inductance and $C$ the capacitance, so the operator is $A = 1/LC$, one number. Kirchhoff's voltage law, which balances voltages as Newton's law balances forces, says that the voltages around a closed loop add to zero. A capacitor holding charge $q$ has the voltage $q/C$ across it; a coil carrying the current $I = \dot q$ has the voltage $L\,\dot I$. Around the loop, $L\,\ddot q + q/C = 0$, that is, $\ddot q = -q/LC$: the coil plays the mass and $1/C$ the spring's stiffness. For ideal parts both laws are linear, so no small-motion step is needed.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>How two radio frequencies make one audible tone</summary>

A mixer multiplies the two oscillators' signals, and $\sin(2\pi f_1t)\sin(2\pi f_2t) = \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 - f_2)t) - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi(f_1 + f_2)t)$; a filter keeps the difference. With both near a few hundred kilohertz, a hand that changes one circuit's capacitance by a small fraction moves the difference across the whole audible range. Real theremins' mixers and circuits add overtones, on the whole-number lines of the difference frequency, since the output repeats at that rate.

</details>
:::

## What each instrument breaks {#breaks}

Post 2's string kept [six conditions](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd#conditions); the others break some:

| Instrument | Which of post 2's conditions it breaks |
|:----|:--------------|
| piano | none while the key is down; the damper breaks *friction the sines split* and *unchanging in time* |
| kalimba | none in the model (its fading is measured) |
| glockenspiel | *$A$ positive*: the two drifts, which the supports hold |
| drums | none on the ideal head; the kettledrum's radiation breaks *$A$ symmetric* |
| violin | *linear*: the bow, which also feeds energy in |
| flute | *linear*: the jet |
| clarinet | *linear*: the reed |
| harmonica | *linear*: the reed's valve |
| theremin | *linear*: the amplifier; a moving hand changes $C$, breaking *unchanging in time* |

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
// One drumhead, two drums: a five-step toy model (bass drum above, timpani below).
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = window.Core;
  var J11 = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.m === 1 && d.n === 1; })[0].j, J01 = C.DR[0].j;
  var MODES = C.DR.filter(function (d) { return d.j / J11 <= 3.6; });
  function kind(d) { return d.m === 0 ? "round" : d.n === 1 ? "spoke" : "other"; }
  var COL = { round: "--pos", spoke: "--neg", other: "--metal" };
  var STEPS = {
    1: ["Same head, same operator", "Both drums start as this entry's operator on a disk with the rim held still. On this ideal head the frequencies fall off the dashed lines, and the two diagrams are identical. Two kinds of mode will matter: the round modes, with no line through the center, and the spoke modes, with lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim."],
    2: ["Where you strike decides which modes start", "A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. A bass drum is struck slightly off center, where the spoke modes barely move, so its lowest modes are mostly round ones. A kettledrum is struck between halfway and three-quarters of the way out, where the lowest round mode starts more weakly than the spoke modes."],
    3: ["The air adds mass, most to coarse shapes", "Air on both sides of the head moves with it. A ripple of wavenumber k drags along a layer of air about 1/k thick, so a coarse mode carries more extra mass and slows down more: f ∝ k / √(σ + 2ρ/k). This happens to both drums. It stretches the spoke modes toward the dashed lines; in this toy model it gets about halfway, and a full calculation of the air gets the rest."],
    4: ["What surrounds each head", "A kettledrum's bowl is nearly sealed, so its air resists only shapes that change the volume it encloses. A mode with lines through the center pushes up as much as it pulls down, sweeps no net volume, and keeps its frequency exactly; only the round modes are raised. A bass drum has no kettle: its second head, coupled through the air in the shell, splits its lowest modes instead (not modelled here)."],
    5: ["What fades", "A round mode pumps air like a piston and radiates its energy away within a fraction of a second. On the bass drum, a strike near the center starts mostly round modes among the lowest ones. How long the rest rings is the player's choice: a leg or a towel on the head muffles every mode under it, for short, dry notes (press Muffle); lift it and the drum rings on. The leftover stems that land near a line are chance near-misses of this toy model, not a set of modes pulled onto the lines, and a real bass drum's second head, coupled through the air in its shell, splits its lowest modes, which the model leaves out. The result is a boom with no clear pitch, as intended. On the kettledrum the spoke modes ring on, near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 times a base an octave below the (1,1): a note. Real timpani sit closer to the lines than this toy model; press Measured ratios to see and hear them."]

<script>
// The orchestra: one instrument from each Hornbostel–Sachs class, drawn and played by orchestra.js.
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var O = window.Orchestra; if (!O) return;
  // On this page each family's card points to its entry below.
  var HERE = { electro: "The theremin: entry below", chord: "The piano: entry below", aero: "The clarinet: entry below", idio: "The glockenspiel: entry below", membrane: "The two drums: entry below" };
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) { if (HERE[f.id]) f.where = HERE[f.id]; });
  var fams = document.getElementById("oFams"), mute = {};
  O.FAM.forEach(function (f) {
    var b = document.createElement("button"); b.type = "button"; b.className = "chip"; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", "true");
    b.style.setProperty("--c", "rgb(" + f.hue.join(",") + ")"); b.innerHTML = '<span class="dot"></span>' + f.inst;
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { mute[f.id] = !mute[f.id]; b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", mute[f.id] ? "false" : "true"); applyMute(f.id); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
    fams.appendChild(b);
  });
  var cv = document.getElementById("oStage"), g = cv.getContext("2d"), timeEl = document.getElementById("oTime");

  tlPerf.mute = mute; tlFull.mute = mute;
  var REST = O.beatToSec(8 * 16 + 4.15);
  function fit() {
    var full = document.fullscreenElement === cv, dpr = Math.min(2, window.devicePixelRatio || 1);
    var w = full ? Math.min(window.innerWidth, window.innerHeight * 16 / 9) : cv.getBoundingClientRect().width;
    w = Math.max(320, Math.round(w * dpr)); cv.width = w; cv.height = Math.round(w * 9 / 16);
  }
  function drawRest() { O.drawAt(g, REST, cv.width, cv.height, tlPerf); }
  function mmss(x) { x = Math.max(0, Math.round(x)); return Math.floor(x / 60) + ":" + ("0" + x % 60).slice(-2); }
  function applyMute(id) { if (fg && ctx) fg[id].gain.setTargetAtTime(mute[id] ? 0 : 1, ctx.currentTime, 0.03); }

    if (!ctx) return;

  }

    if (!AC) { timeEl.textContent = "This browser cannot play Web Audio."; return; }
    ctx = new AC(); if (ctx.resume) ctx.resume();
    var my = ctx; timeEl.textContent = "Computing the sounds…";
    setTimeout(function () {
      if (ctx !== my) return;
      var cache = O.prepare(ctx, cur.notes);
      t0 = ctx.currentTime + 0.2;
      fg = O.schedule(ctx, cur.notes, t0, { cache: cache, mute: mute });
      raf = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
    }, 30);
  }
  document.getElementById("oPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { play(false); });
  document.getElementById("oFull").addEventListener("click", function () { play(true); });
  document.getElementById("oStop").addEventListener("click", stop);
  var fsb = document.getElementById("oFs");
  if (!cv.requestFullscreen) fsb.hidden = true;
  fsb.addEventListener("click", function () { if (cv.requestFullscreen) cv.requestFullscreen().catch(function () {}); });
  document.addEventListener("fullscreenchange", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  window.addEventListener("resize", function () { fit(); if (!ctx) drawRest(); });
  fit(); drawRest();
  var faces = ['700 48px "LM Roman"', 'italic 24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Roman"', '24px "LM Sans"', '24px "LM Math"'];
  if (document.fonts && document.fonts.load) Promise.all(faces.map(function (f) { return document.fonts.load(f, "A−κ♯"); })).then(function () { if (!ctx) drawRest(); }, function () {});
})();
</script>
```
